name: Jet peel (needle-free)

lead: A jet peel uses a pressurised stream of saline, oxygen or serum to treat skin and deliver products without needles. Clinics offer it as a hydration or glow treatment for a smoother, plumper look.

A handheld device propels a fine jet at the skin surface; providers say this lightly exfoliates and drives products in. A small registered comparison of a hydrating treatment and a jet peel for facial hydration (23 participants) is the only related research found, with no results available.

paras: It is done in a clinic session, usually described as low downtime, and often used before events.
No safety data specific to jet peel were found in the sources reviewed.

angle.text: Clinics offer it as a needle-free facial for hydration and a smoother look. A pressurised stream hydrates the skin surface and delivers products, giving plumper-looking skin. Little has been published on it.

lead: A jet peel is an aesthetic facial in which a handheld wand propels a pressurised stream of saline, oxygen or serum across the skin without needles. People book it for a fresher, smoother, more hydrated look, and clinics also use it as a way of working serums into the skin.[1][2] Sessions are short, are described by providers as having little downtime, and are often bought as a series.[2]

Healthline describes the usual session as a wand that cleans the skin with a spray of oxygen and saline, followed by a custom serum, often containing hyaluronic acid, salicylic acid, glycolic acid, vitamin C or B vitamins, that the jet pushes into the skin. Claimed appearance benefits include smoother skin from exfoliation, a more even tone, softer-looking scars, deeper pore cleansing and a reduced look of wrinkles and sun damage.[2] Healthline adds that people have also discussed jet delivery of minoxidil to the scalp and of local anaesthetic, and notes that research on all these uses is limited.[2]

The technology descends from medical jet injectors, which deliver liquid through the skin under high pressure and have been used since the mid-twentieth century for mass vaccination and insulin.[3] Research specific to cosmetic jet peels is limited to one small registered comparison of a hydrating treatment and a jet peel for facial skin hydration.[1]

In salons the jet peel sits in the same market as HydraFacial and similar serum-infusing facials, which Healthline describes as very similar treatments and for which it says there is not enough research to show that one outperforms another.[2]
infobox: Hyaluronic acid, salicylic acid, glycolic acid, vitamin C, B vitamins [2]
About $125-159 per session in one example [2]

paras: Jet peel devices use a high-velocity jet of liquid or gas to treat the skin surface. Providers describe the method as a way of cleansing, lightly exfoliating and applying serums without needles, in short sessions without downtime.[2]
Healthline notes that, despite the name, a jet peel is a non-invasive facial rather than a chemical or laser peel, and that the serum is chosen by the provider to suit the person's skin goals.[2]

Healthline refers to an FDA-cleared device sold as JetPeel, and its cited sources name the JetPeel JP1-N01 and JetPeel-3 models.[2] Providers use the generic term jet peel for treatments from this device family, and the same phrase appears on menus in medical spas and salons.

The name is a misnomer in one respect: Healthline points out that a jet peel is a non-invasive facial rather than a chemical or laser peel, so it does not remove skin in the way a peel does.[2] Its exfoliating effect is described as a light, mechanical one from the stream of liquid and oxygen.[2]

Needle-free jet injection predates cosmetic use. Wikipedia credits the earliest documented device able to push water or medicine through the skin to an invention of Dr. Jean Sales-Girons, presented to the Paris Academie Imperiale de Medecine by Jules-Auguste Beclard in 1866.[3][3]

In 1935 engineer Arnold Sutermeister proposed medical use of high-pressure jets after seeing a worker injured by one; Marshall Lockhart patented a device in 1936, and Lockhart's Hypospray was introduced for clinical evaluation in 1947.[3] The US Army sought devices for rapid mass immunisation from 1951 and made multi-use-nozzle jet injectors its standard in 1961; the CDC used them in polio campaigns, and in 1967 Nicaraguans nicknamed them Peace Guns.[3]

Cosmetic jet peel devices apply the same underlying idea, a fine high-velocity stream, to the skin surface rather than for injection into deeper tissue. Wikipedia's jet injector article does not discuss cosmetic applications, so the link is one of technique rather than of documented product lineage.[3]

Providers recommend jet peels for fine lines, dull or dehydrated skin, congested pores and uneven tone, and some people repeat sessions every two to four weeks, though Healthline says recommendations on frequency are anecdotal.[2]

A 2024 paper in Skin Research and Technology reported on poly-d,l-lactic acid delivered by transdermal microjet for atrophic scars in Asian patients, a related needle-free delivery approach in aesthetics.[4]

Healthline describes a typical jet peel as a wand that cleans the skin with oxygen and saline, after which a provider-selected serum is pushed into the skin; serums commonly contain hyaluronic acid, salicylic acid, glycolic acid, vitamin C or B vitamins.[2] The session is short, involves no needles and is described by providers as having little downtime.[2] Some people repeat sessions every two to four weeks, although Healthline says frequency recommendations are anecdotal.[2]
Jet peels are often discussed alongside other facials that combine cleansing, exfoliation and serum application, such as HydraFacial, which uses a different, suction-based hand piece.[2]

Healthline lists redness, swelling, pain, pustules or cysts, enlarged lymph nodes and infection as possible side effects, with cellulitis rare, and says jet peels are not usually recommended during pregnancy.[2]

Medical jet injectors have a documented history of cross-contamination through splash-back, fluid suck-back and retrograde flow. A 1986 hepatitis B outbreak affected 57 patients at a Los Angeles weight-loss clinic using a Med-E-Jet, and a 1988 podiatry clinic cluster of Mycobacterium chelonae infections followed jet-injected toe anaesthetic; the US Department of Defense stopped using multi-use jet injectors for mass vaccination in 1997, and the WHO no longer recommends them for vaccination.[3][3] Single-use or protected nozzles in modern devices are intended to address this concern, and cosmetic jet peel treatments work on the skin surface rather than as injections.[3][2]
Healthline cites $125 to $159 per session or $300 to $435 for a three-session package, with insurance unlikely to cover it.[2]

One trial registration, NCT07793149, compares a hydrating treatment branded KIRA with jet peel for facial skin hydration and skin rejuvenation in 23 participants; it began in May 2026 and is listed as completed, without published results.[1] A 2024 study examined microjet delivery of poly-d,l-lactic acid for atrophic scars.[4] No other studies on cosmetic jet peel were found.

Healthline describes HydraFacial as very similar to a jet peel, since both exfoliate and infuse serum, and notes that Dermalinfusion uses a diamond-tipped wand and vacuums away debris. It states that there is not enough research to show that any of these treatments is better than the others.[2]

Other needle-free delivery approaches in aesthetics include transdermal microjet systems. A 2024 paper in Skin Research and Technology described poly-d,l-lactic acid delivered by transdermal microjet for atrophic scars in Asian patients.[4] That work concerns a medical-grade microjet device rather than a salon jet peel.

sections.h: Use in beauty and appearance communities
paras: Jet peels are discussed mostly by treatment providers, beauty writers and clients rather than in looksmaxxing forums. The appeal described is a quick, no-needle option before events or as part of a regular skincare routine: hydrated, brighter-looking skin with no recovery period.[2]
Healthline notes that the results are temporary, which is why some clients return every two to four weeks, a schedule it describes as anecdotal rather than evidence-based.[2]

timeline.event: A fluid-injection device without a needle is presented in Paris.[3]
Arnold Sutermeister proposes high-pressure jets for medicine; Marshall Lockhart patents a jet injector the following year.[3]
The Hypospray jet injector is introduced clinically.[3]
The US Army makes multi-use-nozzle jet injectors its standard for immunisation.[3]
The US Department of Defense stops using multi-use jet injectors for mass vaccination.[3]
Healthline publishes a medically reviewed overview of jet peel facials, noting limited research.[2]
A study of poly-d,l-lactic acid delivered by transdermal microjet for atrophic scars is published in Skin Research and Technology.[4]
A registered comparison of a hydrating treatment and jet peel for facial skin hydration (23 participants) begins in May.[1]
